slides.title: Chapter 8: Manipulating Strings
slides.sub: Literals, slices, formatting, methods, bytes and the clipboard - a string never changes in place
slides.notes: Chapters 1 to 7 worked with numbers, lists and dictionaries. This chapter is about the string: how one is written, read and rebuilt into a new string, since no method can ever change the string it was called on. Every example on these slides was run under Python 3.14.6 and the result printed beside it is the result Python gave.

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.sub: The chapter's own competency questions; the summary comes back to each

items: Which operations on a string make a new string, which only test it and return a Boolean or a number, and why can none of them change it?
Which printed outputs and concepts of the chapter differ in current Python, and on what source?
6 branches
66 concepts
77 console rows
Python 3.14.6

slides.notes: The first question is the chapter's spine: a string method either builds a new string, such as upper() and split(), or it only looks at the string and answers with a Boolean or a number, such as isupper() and find(), and the reason is that a string is immutable, so no method ever has a string to change. The second question is this chapter's own watch-out: the chapter was printed before f-strings' debug specifier, before t-strings and before several of the methods now current in Python 3.14, so a few of its claims need a source check against the version actually running. The chips give the size of the chapter.
slides.take: Every string method either returns new or tests; it never changes the string.

slides.title: String literals and quoting
slides.sub: A string is text inside quotes, with an escape for the quote it is inside

items.label: single, double, escapes, bytes and the backslash

items.head: Why two kinds of quotes
items.body: Alice's cat needs double quotes, or the apostrophe inside it must be escaped as \'. The backslash also writes a tab or a newline inside an ordinary string, which a raw string switches off so a Windows path can be typed literally.

slides.notes: A string literal sits inside single or double quotes, and choosing the other kind of quote is the easiest way to hold an apostrophe. The backslash begins an escape sequence: \t is a tab and \n is a newline, both counted as one character by len() though they are two characters in the source. A raw string, written r'...', turns every backslash into a plain character, which is why a Windows path is typed as r'C:\Users\Alice\Desktop' without doubling anything, and a bytes literal, b'a', holds raw bytes rather than text at all.
slides.take: An escape or a raw string decides what a backslash means.

slides.title: Raw strings and multiline strings
slides.sub: A raw string keeps the backslash; triple quotes keep the line breaks

items.label: a raw string keeps every backslash; triple quotes keep every newline

items.body:
r'
' is two characters, a backslash and an n; '
' is one, the newline. letter.split('
') breaks the triple-quoted letter back into its four lines, the blank line between them showing up as ''.

slides.notes:
A raw string is for text where backslashes are meant literally, such as a Windows path or a regular expression pattern, and len(r'
') is 2 while len('
') is 1, because the raw string never turns 
 into a newline character. A triple-quoted string, opened and closed with three quote marks, can run across several lines of source code and keeps every line break and blank line exactly as typed; the console on this slide types the same four-line letter as one REPL line with explicit 
 escapes instead, to the same effect, and splits it back into its lines on '
'.
slides.take: Triple quotes keep line breaks; r-strings keep backslashes.

slides.title: Indexing and slicing
slides.sub: A position finds one character; a colon finds a run of them

items.label: a position finds one character; a slice finds a run of them

items.head: Reading the console
items.body: greeting[0] is the first character and greeting[-1] is the last, counting back from the end. greeting[0:5] takes up to but not including index 5, and greeting[::-1] reverses the whole string by stepping backwards.

slides.notes: Indexing with one number, greeting[4], returns a single character, and a negative index counts from the end, so greeting[-1] is always the last character without knowing the string's length. Slicing with a colon, greeting[0:5], returns every character from the first index up to but not including the second, and either number can be left out to mean the start or the end of the string. A slice with a step of -1, greeting[::-1], walks the string backwards one character at a time and so reverses it, a trick the chapter relies on more than once.
slides.take: Slicing never includes the character at the stop index.

slides.title: The in operator and immutability
slides.sub: in asks whether one string sits inside another; no method changes a string in place

items.label: in tests for a substring; a string cannot be changed in place

items.head: What never changes
items.body: name[0:7] + 'the' + name[8:12] builds a brand new string; it does not edit name. Every method that looks like a change, such as upper(), returns a new string and leaves the original exactly as it was.

slides.notes: The in operator, written 'Hello' in 'Hello, World', tests whether the left string occurs anywhere inside the right one and returns a Boolean, with not in as its opposite; the empty string is found inside every string, so '' in 'spam' is always True. A string is immutable: once created it can never be edited in place, so to change part of a message you slice out the parts you want and concatenate them into a new string with +, exactly as the console does to replace the middle of a cat's name.
slides.take: A string cannot change; every edit builds a new one.

slides.title: F-strings
slides.sub: An f-string evaluates what is inside the braces and substitutes the result

rows: f'My name is {name}. I am {age} years old. In ten years I will be {age + 10}. {{name}}'
'My name is Al. I am 4000 years old. In ten years I will be 4010. {name}'
items.label: an f-string evaluates {expr}; format specifiers and = control how it is shown

items.body: {age + 10} runs the expression first; {42:>6} right-justifies in 6 characters; {name=} prints the expression text and its value together, which the chapter's own printing did not yet have.

slides.notes: Writing f before the opening quote turns a string literal into an f-string, and anything inside braces is evaluated as a Python expression and substituted into the text, so f'{age + 10}' prints 4010 rather than the text age + 10. A format specifier after a colon controls the display, as in {3.14159:.2f} for two decimal places or {255:#x} for hexadecimal, and a double brace, {{name}}, prints a literal brace. The self-documenting {name=} and {age + 1 = } forms, added in Python 3.8, print the expression's own source text beside its value, a convenience the printed chapter could not show because it did not exist when the chapter was written.
slides.take: f'{expr}' evaluates expr and substitutes the result as text.

slides.title: One PEP gave Python its f-string, in a single day

items.head: PEP 498
items.body: Literal String Interpolation. Created 1 August 2015 by Eric V. Smith, targeted at Python 3.6, and its own example reads almost exactly like the chapter's: f'My name is {name}, my age next year is {age+1}'.

items: 1 August 2015: PEP 498 is created, authored by Eric V. Smith
Targeted at Python 3.6, shipped at the end of 2016
The PEP's own example reads almost like the chapter's
Every f'{name}' since has worked the same way

items.where: the Python Enhancement Proposal index, PEP 498

slides.notes: PEP 498, 'Literal String Interpolation', records its own creation date as 1 August 2015, with Eric V. Smith named as its author and Python 3.6 named as the version it targets. The proposal's own example is almost exactly the chapter's: f'My name is {name}, my age next year is {age+1}'. Python 3.6 shipped the feature at the end of 2016, and f'My name is {name}. I am {age} years old.' has worked the same way in every Python release since. The account rests on these sources. PEP 498, 'Literal String Interpolation', peps.python.org/pep-0498 (Created: 01-Aug-2015; Author: Eric V. Smith; Python-Version: 3.6); What's New in Python 3.6. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.
slides.take: The f-string programmers use daily traces to one named PEP.

slides.title: Older ways to build the same string
slides.sub: Concatenation, %-style and str.format() all still work

rows: 'Hello, my name is ' + name + '. I am ' + str(age) + ' years old.'
'Hello, my name is Al. I am 4000 years old.'
'My name is %s. I am %s years old.' % (name, age)
'My name is Al. I am 4000 years old.'
'{1} years ago, {0} was born and named {0}.'.format(name, age)
'4000 years ago, Al was born and named Al.'
items.label: concatenation, %-formatting and str.format() all predate the f-string

items.body: 'Py' 'thon' concatenates two literals that sit next to each other; 3 * 'un' repeats a string; the {1} and {0} in .format() name arguments by position, out of order if needed.

slides.notes: Before f-strings, the chapter builds the same sentence three ways: by concatenating pieces with + and converting the number with str(), with the %-operator and a tuple of values, and with str.format() and numbered placeholders that can repeat an argument, as {0} does twice. All three still run correctly in Python 3.14, so the chapter's own point stands: f-strings are newer and usually clearer, but nothing here was removed. Two adjacent string literals with nothing between them, 'Py' 'thon', are concatenated by the compiler into one string at compile time, and the * operator repeats a string that many times.
slides.take: f-strings replaced none of the three older styles; all still run.

slides.title: Changing case and testing it
slides.sub: upper() and lower() build new strings; isupper() only asks

items.head: casefold vs lower
items.body: 'stra\xdfe'.casefold() == 'strasse' is True because casefold() also expands the German sharp s, something lower() alone does not do; it exists only for comparing text, never for display.

slides.notes: upper() and lower() each return a new string with every letter changed, leaving the original exactly as it was, and isupper() only tests whether the letters already present are all uppercase and returns a Boolean, so 'great' == 'GREat'.lower() is the idiom for a case-insensitive comparison. casefold(), added for stronger comparisons than lower(), also folds special characters such as the German sharp s so that two spellings that a human reads as equal compare as equal; it is meant only for comparison, not for showing text to a reader.
slides.take: casefold() compares text; upper() and lower() build it.

slides.title: Testing a string's content
slides.sub: isalpha, isalnum, isdecimal and the startswith/endswith pair, all Booleans

items.label: isX() methods test every character and answer a Boolean

items.body: startswith/endswith also accept a tuple of several endings to test in one call.

slides.notes: Every is-method tests every character in the string and returns a single Boolean: isalpha() is true only if every character is a letter and the string is not empty, and isalnum() allows letters and digits together. isdecimal() is stricter than it looks: '\u0663'.isdecimal() is True for an Arabic-Indic digit, yet int() on that same character still succeeds, converting it to the ordinary integer 3, a case the chapter's printed text does not show. startswith() and endswith() test one end of the string and, since they accept a tuple, 'notes.txt'.endswith(('.py', '.txt')) checks two endings in a single call.
slides.take: An is-method tests every character and returns one Boolean.

slides.title: Joining and splitting text
slides.sub: join() needs a list of strings; split() and partition() cut one apart

items.label: join() needs a list; split() and partition() cut a string apart

items.body: ', '.join([...]) is called on the separator, with the list as its argument; split() with no argument cuts on any run of whitespace; splitlines() recognises every line boundary split('\n') would miss.

slides.notes: join() is called on the separator string and takes a list of strings to glue together, which is why ', '.join(['cats', 'rats', 'bats']) reads backwards to someone used to other languages. split(sep) cuts a string at every occurrence of sep and returns the pieces as a list; split() with no argument at all is a special case that cuts at any run of whitespace and ignores it at the ends, which is why 'My name is Simon'.split() and split('m') give different results. partition(sep) cuts at only the first occurrence and returns a three-item tuple that keeps the separator itself, where split() would discard it.
slides.take: join() glues a list; split() and partition() cut a string.

slides.title: Justifying and stripping whitespace
slides.sub: rjust/ljust/center pad a string; strip removes characters from its ends

items.label: rjust, ljust, center pad with a fill character; strip removes from the ends

items.body: strip('ampS') removes any of those characters from either end, not the substring 'ampS' as a whole; removesuffix() and removeprefix(), added in Python 3.9, remove one exact piece instead.

slides.notes: rjust() and ljust() pad a string to a given width with spaces or a fill character on one side, and center() pads on both sides, all three used by the chapter's own table-printing program. strip() removes whitespace from both ends by default, and when given a string of characters it removes any of those characters, in any order, from either end until it meets one that is not in the set, which is why strip('ampS') eats through 'SpamSpamBaconSpamEggsSpamSpam' down to 'BaconSpamEggs'. removeprefix() and removesuffix(), added in Python 3.9, are the exact-match tools the chapter's own printed text predates.
slides.take: strip() removes a set of characters; removesuffix() removes one exact piece.

slides.title: Nine companies agree on one table of characters

items.head: The 1991 press release
items.body: Nine companies - Apple, GO, IBM, Metaphor, Microsoft, NeXT, Novell, the Research Libraries Group and Sun - formally affiliated as Unicode Inc. on 19 February 1991, with Xerox's Joe Becker as technical vice president.

items: 19 February 1991: nine companies announce Unicode Inc.
The consortium assigns the numbers ord() and chr() read
ord('A') is 65 because that table says so
The same table underlies the chapter's utf-8 encoding

items.who: Apple, GO, IBM, Metaphor, Microsoft, NeXT, Novell, the Research Libraries Group and Sun Microsystems

slides.notes: On 19 February 1991 a press release from Mountain View announced that nine computer companies had formally affiliated as Unicode Inc., with board members from Apple, GO, IBM, Metaphor, Microsoft, NeXT, Novell, the Research Libraries Group and Sun Microsystems, and Xerox's Joe Becker named as the new consortium's technical vice president. The table of code points this group began maintaining is exactly what ord() and chr() read from today: ord('A') is 65 and chr(8364) is the euro sign because the Unicode Consortium assigned those numbers to those characters. The account rests on these sources. 'Major Computer Companies Join to Promote Worldwide Standard Character Encoding', Unicode Inc. press release, 19 February 1991 (unicode.org/history/first-pr.htm); Python documentation, the unicodedata module. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.
slides.take: ord() and chr() read a table nine companies agreed on in 1991.

slides.title: Finding and replacing
slides.sub: find() returns an index or -1; replace() swaps every occurrence

items.label: find() returns an index or -1; replace() swaps matches

items.head: find vs index
items.body: find() returns -1 for no match, where the related index() method raises a ValueError instead; a third argument to find() starts the search partway through the string.

slides.notes: find() searches for a substring and returns the index of its first occurrence, or -1 if it is not there at all, and an optional second argument starts the search from a later position, which is how the same call finds a second 'spam' further along the string. count() returns how many times a substring occurs, without overlapping matches. replace() returns a new string with every occurrence of the first argument swapped for the second, and an optional third argument limits how many replacements are made, as in replacing only the first of three occurrences of 'spam' with 'eggs'.
slides.take: find() locates a match; replace() swaps every one by default.

slides.title: ord(), chr() and UTF-8 encoding
slides.sub: A code point names a character; UTF-8 turns characters into bytes

items.label: ord()/chr() convert a character to and from its code point; encode() turns text into bytes

items.body: 'caf\xe9'.encode('utf-8') is 5 bytes for 4 characters, since e-acute takes two bytes in utf-8; encoding with errors='replace' swaps an unencodable character for a placeholder instead of raising.

slides.notes: Every character has a code point, a number the Unicode standard assigns to it, and ord() and chr() convert between a character and that number in either direction. Encoding turns text into bytes for a particular scheme: utf-8 is the right choice almost all of the time, because it can represent every Unicode character and stays compatible with plain ASCII, though a character outside ASCII, such as e-acute, can take more than one byte, so len() of the text and len() of its utf-8 encoding can differ. Encoding to plain ascii raises a UnicodeEncodeError on a character ascii cannot hold, unless an errors argument such as 'replace' is given.
slides.take: utf-8 represents every character; ascii cannot.

slides.title: The encoding written on a diner placemat

items.head: Rob Pike's own account
items.body: 'Designed, in front of my eyes, on a placemat in a New Jersey diner one night in September or so 1992... I very clearly remember Ken writing on the placemat.'

items: September 1992: Thompson and Pike sketch UTF-8
Bell Labs, for the Plan 9 operating system
1 to 4 bytes per character, ASCII stays compatible
That is the encoding behind str.encode('utf-8')

items.who: Ken Thompson and Rob Pike, Bell Labs

slides.notes: In September 1992 Ken Thompson and Rob Pike were designing a new encoding for the Plan 9 operating system at Bell Labs. Rob Pike later wrote that UTF-8 'was designed, in front of my eyes, on a placemat in a New Jersey diner one night in September or so 1992', and that he 'very clearly remember[s] Ken writing on the placemat'. The scheme they sketched that night let a character take from one to four bytes while staying compatible with plain ASCII, which is why 'caf\xe9'.encode('utf-8') is five bytes for four characters. That same encoding is what the chapter calls the right choice 99 percent of the time. The account rests on these sources. Rob Pike, 'UTF-8 history', doc.cat-v.org/bell_labs/utf-8_history (first-hand account, dated September 1992); Al Sweigart, Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition (2025), chapter 8. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.
slides.take: The encoding behind str.encode('utf-8') began on a placemat.

slides.title: The Pig Latin program
slides.sub: Vowel-starting words get yay; consonants move to the end and get ay

lines: new_word = word + 'yay'          # starts with a vowel: just add yay
new_word = word + prefix_consonants + 'ay'   # move the consonants to the end, add ay
items.label: program pigLatin_v1_0_0.py, lines 25 to 37 of 41 - Python 3.14.6

items.out:
My name is Al Sweigart. I am 4,000 years old.
Ymay amenay isyay Alyay Eigartsway. IYAY amyay 4,000 yearsyay oldyay.
items.label: typed: My name is Al Sweigart. I am 4,000 years old.

slides.notes: Pig Latin moves the leading consonants of a word to its end and adds ay, or simply adds yay to a word that starts with a vowel, and the program keeps any leading or trailing punctuation untouched around the word it transforms. Typed against 'My name is Al Sweigart. I am 4,000 years old.' the program printed 'Ymay amenay isyay Alyay Eigartsway. IYAY amyay 4,000 yearsyay oldyay.', and the single-letter word 'I' becomes the all-capital 'IYAY' rather than a capitalised 'Iyay', because the program's own case-restoring rule treats a fully uppercase one-letter word as upper rather than title case; a genuine, worth-noticing quirk of the algorithm, not a bug the demonstration hides.
slides.take: A one-letter word exposes Pig Latin's own case quirk, IYAY.

slides.title: Practice: printing a table, alternating case
slides.sub: Column widths come from the data itself, not from a fixed number

lines: col_widths = [0] * len(table_data)         # the widest string of each column, so far 0
items.out:
apples Alice  dogs 
 oranges   Bob  cats 
cherries Carol moose 
  banana David goose
items.label: program tablePrinter_v1_0_0.py, lines 1 to 17 of 17 - Python 3.14.6

items.body: col_widths[i] grows to the longest string in each column, and rjust() uses that width for every row.

slides.notes: The table-printing program computes the widest string in each column before printing a single row, so the table lines up whatever the data happens to be, rather than assuming a fixed width. Each cell is right-justified to its column's own width with rjust() and printed with a trailing space, which is why the four columns of names and animals line up exactly as shown. A second practice program, alternating case, walks a string by position with enumerate() and lowercases even-indexed characters while uppercasing odd ones, turning 'Hello, world!' into 'hElLo, WoRlD!'.
slides.take: Measuring the data first is what makes the table line up.

slides.title: The clipboard and pyperclip
slides.sub: copy() and paste() read and write the operating system's own clipboard

items.head: Two functions, one clipboard
items.body: pyperclip.copy(text) places text on the clipboard and pyperclip.paste() returns whatever is there. The bullet-point-adder program pastes, edits every line, and copies the result back.

items.head: A real limitation, kept honest
items.body: Running the bullet-point-adder program in this headless session raised ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pyperclip', then, once installed, pyperclip.PyperclipException because no clipboard mechanism exists without a desktop. The program is correct; the sandbox has no clipboard.

slides.notes: pyperclip is a third-party module the chapter installs with pip, and its two functions, copy() and paste(), are the entire interface: paste() returns the text currently on the operating system's clipboard as a string, and copy() places a string there for the next paste anywhere on the machine. The bullet-point-adder program pastes whatever text was copied, adds an asterisk and a space to the front of every line, and copies the result back, so the next paste anywhere, in any application, has the bulleted version. This slide's own right-hand card is an honest record of a real error this session hit trying to run that exact program without a desktop clipboard, rather than a claim the program was never actually run.
slides.take: copy() and paste() are pyperclip's whole interface.

slides.title: The chapter's clipboard model is fifty years old

items.head: Larry Tesler, Xerox PARC
items.body: Joined PARC in 1973 and, with Tim Mott, gave the Gypsy word processor its cut, copy and paste model: select, hold, insert elsewhere. Tesler died 16 February 2020, and his obituaries used his own invention as the headline.

items: 1973: Tesler and Mott build the Gypsy word processor
Select, hold, insert elsewhere: cut, copy, paste
16 February 2020: Tesler dies, aged 74
pyperclip.copy()/paste() are the same model, in Python

items.who: Larry Tesler, with Tim Mott, Xerox PARC

slides.notes: Larry Tesler joined Xerox PARC in 1973 and, working with Tim Mott on the Gypsy word processor, gave computing the cut, copy and paste model: select some text, move it to a holding place, and insert it somewhere else. pyperclip.copy() and pyperclip.paste(), the two functions the chapter's clipboard programs call, are that same fifty-year-old model, now reached from three lines of Python instead of a menu. Tesler died on 16 February 2020, at 74, and newspapers around the world wrote his obituary headline with the very model he had invented: 'the inventor of copy and paste'. The account rests on these sources. 'Larry Tesler', Wikipedia, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Tesler (PARC from 1973; the Gypsy word processor with Tim Mott; died 16 February 2020); Al Sweigart, Automate the Boring Stuff with Python, 3rd edition (2025), chapter 8, the pyperclip module. Photo: Wikimedia Commons.
slides.take: pyperclip's two calls are a fifty-year-old idea in Python.

slides.title: The chapter in six lines
slides.sub: One line for each part of the route

items: A literal is quoted text; an escape or a raw string decides what a backslash means inside it.
A position or a slice reads part of a string; in tests for a substring; nothing ever edits one in place.
f-strings evaluate {expr} and substitute it; concatenation, %-style and .format() still work too.
upper()/lower() build new strings, is-methods only test, and casefold() is for comparing text.
join() glues a list; split(), splitlines() and partition() cut a string apart in different ways.
ord()/chr() read a code point; utf-8 encodes it to bytes; pyperclip's copy()/paste() reach the clipboard.

slides.notes: These six lines answer the route one part at a time. The first two cover how a string is written and read, the third and fourth cover building and testing it, the fifth covers cutting and joining text, and the sixth covers bytes and the clipboard. If a line feels unproven, the part of the route that carries it has the slides with the executed examples.
slides.take: If a line feels unproven, its slides hold the example.
